⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧, whose name means who is like the Lord, was a countryman. He came from ⟦l:moresheth_819|Moresheth⟧, a small town in the low hills of the ⟦l:shephelah_1074|Shephelah⟧, about twenty-five miles south-west of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, in the border country between Judah and the old Philistine cities. It was farming land, dotted with fortified towns that guarded the approaches to the capital, and it lay directly in the path of any army marching up from the coast. Micah's prophecy is full of that landscape and its people.

After the story of ⟦p:jonah_1689|Jonah⟧, set in the early years of the eighth century when ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ was still distant, ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ brings us into the decades when it arrived on Judah's doorstep.

The book dates his ministry to the reigns of ⟦p:jotham_1735|Jotham⟧, ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧ and ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧, kings of Judah, roughly the last third of the eighth century before Christ. That makes him a younger contemporary of ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ and Amos, and a contemporary of ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧. Isaiah moved among kings and courtiers in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧; ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ spoke for the small farmers and villagers. Yet the two prophets share a great deal, and one famous passage, about the nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord, appears in almost the same words in both books.

These were the years when ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ swallowed the kingdoms of the west one by one. The listener knows the outline from the second book of Kings. Under ⟦p:ahaz_118|Ahaz⟧, Judah became a vassal of Assyria in return for help against Israel and ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, and Ahaz even had a copy made for the temple of an altar he had seen in Damascus, where he went to meet the Assyrian king. In about seven hundred and twenty-two before Christ, ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ fell, as ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ foretold at the very start of his book. Ahaz's son ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ tore down the high places and led a reform of worship, and later he rebelled against Assyria, and in seven hundred and one ⟦p:sennacherib_2489|Sennacherib⟧ invaded Judah. His own annals boast that he captured forty-six walled towns, and the reliefs from his palace at ⟦l:nineveh_899|Nineveh⟧ show the siege of ⟦l:lachish_711|Lachish⟧, only a few miles from Micah's home. ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ itself was spared, as the books of Kings and ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ relate.

⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧'s chief concern is what was happening inside Judah. Powerful men lay awake planning how to seize their neighbours' fields and houses. Judges and priests took bribes, prophets preached peace to anyone who fed them, and the rulers used their power to devour the people they were meant to protect. All the while, they assured themselves that the Lord was among them and no harm could come. Micah's answer was that ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ would be ploughed like a field.

A century later that word was still remembered. When ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ was on trial for his life for predicting the temple's destruction, some of the elders of Judah reminded the crowd that ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ of ⟦l:moresheth_819|Moresheth⟧ had said the same thing in the days of ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧. Hezekiah had not killed him, they said, but had sought the Lord, and the disaster was turned aside.

The book moves back and forth between judgement and hope, and its three main sections each open with a call to hear. Again and again, after the harshest warnings, comes a promise: a remnant gathered like sheep, ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧ raised up as the place where the nations learn the Lord's ways, and a ruler born in ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, the little town of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s family. After a line naming the prophet and his times, the book opens on a courtroom of cosmic scale. All the peoples of the earth are summoned to hear, and the Lord comes down from his dwelling place, the mountains melting beneath his feet. The charge is against both of his people's capitals. ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ is the sin of the north, and ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ has become the high place of Judah, a name for the hilltop shrines of idolatry.

⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧'s fate comes first. It will become a heap of stones in an open field, fit only for planting vines, a word spoken before the city fell to ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧. But the wound will not stop at the border. It has reached the very gate of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ responds with personal grief, and then with a lament full of wordplay on the towns of his own district. Beth-leaphrah means house of dust, so its people should roll in the dust. ⟦l:lachish_711|Lachish⟧, the great fortress, should harness its horses. The list traces an invader advancing through Micah's homeland towards the capital.

⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ turns now from the coming invasion to its cause, beginning with the landowners who lie awake at night devising schemes and carry them out at first light, because they have the power to do it. They covet fields and seize them, and take away a man's house and his inheritance.

In Israel the land was a family's portion, given by God and meant to stay in the family for generations. The judgement fits the crime. Those who took other people's land will lose their own, and no one will be left to measure out their portion in the assembly of the Lord.

The prophet's hearers do not want to hear any of this. Do not preach, they tell him, disgrace will not overtake us. ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ replies with biting sarcasm: a man who came prophesying wine and strong drink would be just the preacher for them.

Then, abruptly, the tone changes, as it often does in this book. The Lord promises to gather the remnant of his people like sheep in a fold, and to go before them himself as their king.

This chapter brings together three oracles aimed at the nation's leaders. The rulers come first. They should know justice, ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ says, yet they hate good and love evil, and he pictures them as butchers, stripping the people's flesh and chopping their bones for the pot.

Next he turns to the prophets who lead the people astray. They proclaim peace as long as they are fed, and declare war on anyone who will not pay. For them night is coming, with no vision and no answer from God. In contrast ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ describes his own calling: he is filled with power by ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of the Lord, to declare to ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧ his transgression.

The final oracle gathers up the whole leadership, rulers, priests and prophets alike, all working for money while claiming that the Lord is among them. It ends with the most startling word in the book, the one still remembered in ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧'s day. ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧ will be ploughed like a field, and the temple mount will become a wooded ridge.

Immediately after the warning that the temple mount will become a wooded ridge, the book looks far ahead to a different future. In the last days, that same mountain will be raised above every other, and the nations will stream to it to learn the ways of the God of ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧. They will beat their swords into ploughshares, and each man will sit under his own vine and fig tree. Almost the same words appear in the second chapter of ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧.

The rest of the chapter alternates between distress and deliverance. The Lord will gather the lame and the outcast and make them a strong nation. ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧ is pictured as a woman in labour. Then a surprising name appears. You will go to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, ⟦p:micah_2053|Micah⟧ says, and there you will be rescued. In Micah's day Babylon was a restless subject of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, not yet the empire that would one day carry Judah into exile.

The chapter opens with ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ under siege and its ruler humiliated, struck on the cheek with a rod.

The third part of the book opens like the first, with a call to hear. The Lord brings a case against his people, with the mountains and the foundations of the earth as witnesses.

His charge begins with a question, my people, what have I done to you, and then recalls their story: the exodus from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, the leadership of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧, the time when ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧ king of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ hired ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ to curse Israel and Balaam blessed them instead, and the crossing from ⟦l:shittim_1086|Shittim⟧, east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, to ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧, the first camp in the promised land.

The final chapter begins with the prophet's lament. He is like someone searching a vineyard after the harvest and finding nothing left. The godly have vanished, the prince and the judge demand bribes, and no one can be trusted, not even within the family. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would draw on these lines when he warned that a man's enemies would be those of his own household.
